description:
Eclipsar is a team of six students from Bukhara Presidential School in Uzbekistan, and NASA Space Apps 2025 Global Nominees.

We are developers, analysts and problem-solvers who have proved ourselves in olympiads, hackathons and international competitions, and we work best when our different skills meet in one project.
We came to Space Apps 2025 to compete with the world, and we’re back in 2026 to go further.
summary: TerraScope is an Earth system trend detective that runs entirely in the browser on live NASA data. You pick a measure, a place and the years (for example, vegetation in Uzbekistan since 2015), and TerraScope reads one NASA map per month, tests every pixel and the whole area for a real trend, ranks the places that changed most, and says plainly when a change is not significant. It covers 29 measures of land, water, snow, air and sea, checks NASA’s records against ground weather stations, and suggests possible causes with their evidence. It is written in plain words for students and the public, so anyone can see what is changing on Earth, where, how fast, and whether it is real.
details:
What it does
TerraScope answers the four questions of the challenge: what is changing, where, how much, and is it significant.

  • Choose anything, anywhere. 29 measures (vegetation, surface heat, rainfall, soil moisture, snow, open water, dust, gases, sea temperature and more) for any country, lake, sea, continent, searched place or area drawn on the map. Several places can be combined into one area.
  • Find the hotspots. It reads monthly NASA maps from 2000 onwards, turns each pixel into one value per year for the chosen months (so the seasons cannot fake a trend), and groups the pixels that changed into ranked hotspots on the map.
  • Test whether it is real. Every area, hotspot and pixel gets a Mann–Kendall trend test and Sen’s slope with a 95% confidence range. The test allows for years that carry over into the next, pixels are held to a 5% false discovery rate, and a chance check shuffles the years to show whether chance alone could produce hotspots as strong. Two periods can be compared with Welch’s t-test. When a trend is not significant, TerraScope says so and estimates how many more years of data it would need.
  • Look for possible causes. For a clear change, it checks NASA’s records for drier, wetter, warmer or windier years, fire, one-off events and population growth, and lists up to three causes that fit, each with its evidence. It never names “the” cause.
  • Check against the ground. NASA’s air temperature and rainfall trends are compared with the nearest NOAA weather station.
  • World change atlas. A map of where six headline measures changed most since 2003.

Example results measured with the app

  • The Aral Sea’s summer open water fell from 21,970 km² (2003) to 5,020 km² (2026): −690 km² a year, p < 0.001.
  • The Mediterranean’s night-time sea surface temperature rose by +0.61 °C per decade (2003–2025, p = 0.024).
  • Uzbekistan’s vegetation shows no clear trend as a whole, but a significant decline on the Amu Darya delta beside the dried-up Aral Sea.

How it works
For each month, TerraScope requests a map image of the area from NASA GIBS and turns it back into physical values, pixel by pixel, using NASA’s published colour scales. All statistics run in the browser. There is no backend, no API key and no simulated numbers. Results can be shared as a link, downloaded as CSV or saved as a PDF report.

Honest limits
Values are decoded from the colour bins of NASA’s map images, so their precision is that of the colour scale. MERRA-2 is a model constrained by observations at about 50 km. Cloud gaps in MODIS data are left as gaps. The app states these limits wherever they apply.

Tools and languages
TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, three.js, Recharts, Vitest.
